entry: Development of the delta region of [[Bengal]] in South Asia, from the [[Chalcolithic|Chalcolithic period]] to the present. Islam arrived in the 8th century and became dominant from the early 13th century, after conquests led by Bakhtiyar Khalji and missionaries such as Shah Jalal. The Bengal Sultanate ruled from the 14th century, and the region later became part of the [[Mughal Empire]]. After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 it was conquered by the [[East India Company]], and Bengal played a major role in the [[Industrial Revolution]] in Britain. The partition of India in August 1947 made the region East Pakistan. A proclamation of independence in March 1971 led to the nine-month [[Bangladesh Liberation War]]. Military rule under Ziaur Rahman and Hussain Muhammad Ershad was followed by parliamentary democracy, with power alternating between the Awami League and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party. Garment exports and remittances drove growth amid political instability.

Development of the South American territory that became the largest contiguous state in the Americas, from indigenous settlement to the present. Indigenous tribes had lived in the region for thousands of years before Portuguese explorers led by [[Pedro Álvares Cabral]] arrived on April 22, 1500. Brazil was a colony and integral part of the [[Portuguese Empire]] from the 16th to the early 19th century. On September 7, 1822, Prince Regent Pedro declared independence from [[Portugal]], creating the [[Empire of Brazil]]. A military coup in 1889 ended the monarchy, and a 1930 coup brought [[Getúlio Vargas]] to power as an authoritarian ruler until 1945. Democracy was briefly restored until a military coup in 1964, supported by the [[United States]], established another dictatorship. Under Emílio Garrastazu Médici from 1969 to 1974 the economy grew in what was called the Brazilian Miracle. The military regime ended in 1985, and civilian democracy was restored.

Development of the religion founded in ancient India, from the 5th century BCE to the present. [[Buddhism]] originated in and around the Kingdom of [[Magadha]] and is based on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama. It spread from northeastern India across Central, East and Southeast Asia, and at one time influenced most of Asia. Early disputes led to councils and to a first schism between the Sthavira and Mahasamghika groups, traditionally attributed to disagreements over monastic discipline. Under the Mauryan emperor [[Ashoka]], monks were sent to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. Numerous movements arose, among them the [[Mahayana]], [[Theravada]] and [[Vajrayana]] traditions, which spread along the [[Silk Road]] and into Tibet, Southeast Asia and East Asia. Buddhism declined on the Indian subcontinent during the medieval period, as Hindu traditions absorbed it and Turkic-Muslim raids destroyed monasteries such as Nalanda in 1193.

Development of the territory of [[Canada]] from the arrival of [[Paleo-Indians]] thousands of years ago to the present. Indigenous peoples had lived there for millennia. From the late 15th century, French and British expeditions explored and fought over the region. Jacques Cartier claimed the colony of New France in 1534, and permanent settlements began in 1608. Under the 1763 Treaty of Paris, France ceded nearly all its North American possessions to Great Britain after the [[Seven Years' War]]. The Province of Canada joined [[New Brunswick]] and [[Nova Scotia]] in Confederation in 1867, and over the next 82 years the country expanded to include [[Newfoundland and Labrador]] in 1949. The Statute of Westminster in 1931 recognized Canada as co-equal with the United Kingdom, and the Patriation of the Constitution in 1982 removed legal dependence on the British parliament. Canada is now a parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy of ten provinces and three territories.

Development of the peoples and states of [[Central Asia]], from prehistory to the present. Aridity and distance from the sea made agriculture difficult and limited trade, so few major cities developed, and nomadic horse peoples of the steppe dominated the region for millennia. Steppe horse archers launched conquests into settled areas, and the [[Mongol Empire]] conquered much of Eurasia. Firearms allowed settled powers to end nomadic dominance from the 16th century. The [[Russian Empire]] and the [[Qing dynasty]] of China seized most of the region by the end of the 19th century, and the [[Soviet Union]] incorporated most of it after the Russian Revolution of 1917. Soviet rule brought industrialization but suppressed local cultures. After the Soviet collapse in 1991, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, [[Kyrgyzstan]] and Tajikistan became independent. Former communist officials kept power as local strongmen in most of the new states, while Kyrgyzstan ousted three presidents in popular uprisings without consolidating a stable democracy.

Development of one of the world's oldest civilizations, from its origins in the Yellow and [[Yangtze]] river basins to the present. The earliest confirmed period is the [[Shang dynasty]] (c. 1250 BC), followed by the [[Zhou dynasty]], which introduced the [[Mandate of Heaven]] and the foundations of Confucianism, Taoism and Legalism. [[Qin Shi Huang]] first unified China under a centralized imperial state in 221 BC. The Han dynasty (202 BC–220 AD) institutionalized Confucianism, and the Tang (618–907) and Song (960–1279) were eras of cultural flourishing. The [[Mongol Empire]] conquered China in the 13th century, and the Ming (1368–1644) and Qing (1644–1912) dynasties followed. The 1911 Revolution ended imperial rule. After the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Chinese Civil War, [[Mao Zedong]] proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949, while the Republic of China government retreated to Taiwan. Reform and opening up under [[Deng Xiaoping]] from 1978 transformed the country into the world's fastest-growing major economy.

Development of the religion based on the life and teachings of [[Jesus]], from the first century to the present. Christianity began among Jewish communities in Judea and grew into a mostly urban movement of over a million adherents by the third century. [[Constantine the Great]] issued the Edict of Milan in 313, legalizing it, and the Nicene Creed of 325 addressed competing doctrines. After the fall of Rome in 476, monks preserved learning, while [[Early Muslim conquests]] devastated many Christian communities in the Middle East and North Africa. The [[East–West Schism]] of 1054 separated Eastern Orthodoxy from the Catholic Church. The [[Reformation]] of the 16th century, begun by [[Martin Luther]], produced Protestantism. Christianity spread through the colonization of the Americas, Australia and New Zealand. In the 20th century it declined in most of the Western world while growing in the Global South, particularly Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa.

Development of the nation in [[South America]] from its settlement by hunter-gatherers to the present. Agrarian societies emerged between 5000 and 1000 BCE, and the Muisca formed a confederation on the high plateau with one of the most developed political systems in South America, surpassed only by the Incas. The [[Spain|Spanish]] arrived in 1499 and created the Viceroyalty of New Granada, with its capital at [[Bogotá]]. Independence was won in 1819, but the [[Gran Colombia]] federation was dissolved in 1830, and what is now Colombia and Panama became the Republic of New Granada. The Republic of Colombia was declared in 1886 after experiments with federalism. Panama seceded in 1903. Since the 1960s the country has suffered an asymmetric low-intensity armed conflict, which escalated in the 1990s and decreased from 2005 onward. A 2016 peace accord demobilized the FARC's 7,000 fighters, though dissident factions and the ELN persisted.

Development of the region including [[China]], Japan, Korea, Mongolia and Taiwan, from prehistory to the present. Scholars regard East Asia as a distinct cultural region, one defined by adherence to Confucianism, the influence of Buddhism and the use of chopsticks. Recorded civilization began around 2000 BC in the [[Shang dynasty]] along the [[Yellow River]], and Gojoseon became the first organized state in Korea around 195 BC. Japan emerged as a unitary state with its first constitution in 604 AD. Under the Sui, Tang and Song, China was the most advanced civilization in East Asia. The Mongol Empire under [[Genghis Khan]], [[Subutai]] and [[Kublai Khan]] brought most of the region under one state, except Japan and Taiwan, and the Yuan dynasty's two invasions of Japan failed. The Ming and Joseon dynasties adopted Neo-Confucianism, while Japan fell into the Sengoku Jidai civil war, which lasted over a century and a half.

Development of one of the world's oldest civilizations, along the [[Nile]], from prehistory to the present. Egypt was unified around 3150 BC by King [[Narmer]], and dynastic rule lasted for about three millennia with a distinctive religion, arts, language and customs. The Old Kingdom built the pyramids, including those of Djoser and at Giza. Persian, Greek, Roman and Arab rule followed, and Egypt was joined to the [[Ottoman Empire]] in 1517. Britain controlled Egypt in the late 19th century. The 1952 Free Officers' revolution abolished the monarchy, and a republic was proclaimed in 1953 with [[Gamal Abdel Nasser]] rising to leadership. [[Anwar Sadat]] made a peace treaty with Israel in 1979. After the 2011 uprising ousted Hosni Mubarak, the [[Muslim Brotherhood]] governed briefly under Mohamed Morsi, who was removed in a 2013 counter-coup led by [[Abdel Fattah el-Sisi]], who now leads the country.

Development of one of Africa's oldest countries, from ancient kingdoms in the [[Horn of Africa]] to the present. In the 1st century AD the [[Kingdom of Aksum|Aksumite Kingdom]] grew into a major power on the [[Red Sea]], and under King Ezana in the early 4th century Christianity became the state religion. Aksum declined with the rise of Islam in Arabia, and the Zagwe dynasty built a new capital at Lalibela before the Solomonic dynasty took over in the 13th century. The decisive victory at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, under [[Menelik II]], preserved sovereignty during the [[Scramble for Africa]]. Fascist Italy occupied the country from 1936 to 1941. Emperor [[Haile Selassie]] modernized the state and championed African independence at the [[League of Nations]]. A 1974 coup brought the [[Derg]] military council to power, and its Marxist-Leninist regime was responsible for the Red Terror and the 1984–85 famine until it was overthrown in 1991.

Development of the western European territory once known as [[Gaul]], from the Iron Age to the present. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul in the Gallic Wars of 58–51 BC, and it became integrated into the Roman Empire. [[Clovis I]] united most of Gaul in the late 5th century, and Frankish power peaked under [[Charlemagne]]. The [[Hundred Years' War]] ended in a Valois victory in 1453 after [[Joan of Arc]] led French forces. Under [[Louis XIV]] France became a centralized absolute monarchy, and the [[French Revolution]] overthrew the monarchy in the late 18th century. After regime changes, the Third Republic was established in 1870. France played a decisive role in defeating the Central Powers in World War I, but was conquered by Nazi Germany in 1940, and the Fourth Republic was established after liberation in 1944. After the 1958 Algerian crisis, [[Charles de Gaulle]] established the Fifth Republic, and most of the colonial empire became independent.

Development of the central European region now forming the Federal Republic of Germany, from the Paleolithic to the present. Germanic tribes resisted Roman annexation, and in 962 Otto I became the first emperor of the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. The Reformation, begun by [[Martin Luther]] after 1517, divided the empire along religious lines, and the [[Thirty Years' War]] (1618–48) brought great destruction. The Holy Roman Empire dissolved in 1806 during the Napoleonic Wars. [[Otto von Bismarck]] unified Germany as the German Empire in 1871. After defeat in World War I, the Weimar Republic was established. In 1933 [[Adolf Hitler]] established a totalitarian regime, and the Nazis committed the Holocaust, which killed 11 million people, including 6 million Jews. After 1945 Germany was divided into the NATO-aligned West Germany and the Warsaw Pact-aligned East Germany. The [[Berlin Wall]] was opened in 1989, and the two states were reunited.

Development of the Greek people and the lands they inhabited, from prehistory to the present. Bronze Age Greece saw the rise of the [[Minoan civilization]] on Crete and the Mycenaean palace culture, which ended in the [[Late Bronze Age collapse]]. Classical Greece was a world of independent city-states such as [[Athens]] and [[Sparta]], and inter-Greek conflicts included the [[Peloponnesian War]]. The conquests of [[Alexander the Great]] spread Greek culture across the Near East. After Roman rule from 146 BC, the [[Byzantine Empire]] preserved Greek learning until the [[Fall of Constantinople]] in 1453. Ottoman rule ended with the Greek uprising of 1821. Independence was followed by the Balkan Wars and two world wars, a civil conflict (1946–1949) and a military junta (1967–1974), before democratic consolidation and European integration. Most Greeks now live in Greece and Cyprus.

Development of the religious traditions native to the Indian subcontinent, from the [[Indus Valley Civilisation|Indus Valley Civilization]] to the present. Scholars regard Hinduism as a synthesis of many Indian cultures and traditions, with no single founder, which emerged around the start of the [[Common Era]]. The Vedic religion came with Indo-Aryan migrations between 1900 and 1400 BCE, and the [[Vedas]] were composed. The Epics and the first Puranas were composed c. 200 BCE–500 CE, and the [[Gupta Empire|Gupta-era]] classical period (c. 320–650 CE) saw six branches of philosophy evolve. The Bhakti movement gave rise to [[Shaivism]] and [[Vaishnavism]], and [[Adi Shankara]] became the main proponent of Advaita Vedanta. Hindu reform movements emerged in the colonial period, and the [[Partition of India]] of 1947, along religious lines, left the Republic of India with a Hindu majority. Hindu diaspora communities now exist on every continent, with the largest in the United States and the United Kingdom.

Political, economic and social development of the [[South Asia|South Asian]] state since independence in 1947. Independence on 15 August 1947 came with the partition of the British Raj into India and Pakistan, which caused a population transfer of more than 10 million people. [[Jawaharlal Nehru]] became the first prime minister, and the constitution adopted in 1950 made India a democratic republic. India fought wars with [[Pakistan]] over [[Kashmir]] in 1947–1948, 1965, 1971 and 1999, and a war with [[China]] in 1962. It was neutral during the [[Cold War]] and a leader of the [[Non-Aligned Movement]], but drew closer to the [[Soviet Union]] after 1971. India conducted its first nuclear test in 1974 and five more in 1998. Socialist-inspired policies from the 1950s to the 1980s brought regulation and slow growth, and economic liberalization began in 1991. India is now described as the sixth largest economy by nominal GDP and the fastest-growing major economy.

Development of the [[Indian subcontinent]] from the arrival of modern humans to independence in 1947. The [[Indus Valley Civilisation|Indus Valley Civilization]] flourished between 2500 and 1900 BCE in present-day Pakistan and northwestern India, and Indo-Aryan tribes moved in around 1800–1500 BCE. Around 600 BCE, the rise of Jainism and Buddhism marked a second urbanization. [[Chandragupta Maurya]] founded the first great empire of ancient India, the [[Maurya Empire]], and its king [[Ashoka]] embraced Buddhism after the violent Kalinga War. The Delhi Sultanate was established in 1206, and the [[Mughal Empire]] conquered most of the subcontinent in the 16th century. The [[East India Company]] gained control of large parts of India between the mid-18th and mid-19th centuries, and the 1857 rebellion led to direct rule by the British Crown in the British Raj. The Indian National Congress led an independence struggle under Mahatma Gandhi, and the British Indian Empire was partitioned in August 1947.

Development of the archipelago of more than 17,000 islands in [[Southeast Asia]], from prehistory to the present. Austronesian peoples arrived around 2000 BCE. The Hindu and Buddhist [[Srivijaya]] kingdom flourished from the 7th century, followed by the Hindu [[Majapahit]] kingdom in the late 13th century. Islam became dominant in [[Java]] and Sumatra by the end of the 16th century. The [[Dutch East India Company]] (VOC) became the dominant European power by 1610 until it was dissolved in 1800. Japanese occupation in 1942–1945 ended Dutch rule, and two days after Japan's surrender in August 1945, nationalist leader [[Sukarno]] declared independence. After an attempted coup in 1965 and an army-led anti-communist purge that killed over half a million people, [[Suharto]] became president in 1968. His New Order was marked by corruption and human rights abuses, and Suharto resigned in 1998 amid the East Asian financial crisis, after which democratic reforms followed.

Development of the civilizations of the [[Iranian plateau]], also known as Persia, from prehistory to the present. Settlements date to the 5th millennium BC. The Medes unified the region as a kingdom in the 7th century BC, and [[Cyrus the Great]] founded the [[Achaemenid Empire]] by 550 BC, the largest empire yet seen. After Alexander's conquest came Seleucid rule and then the [[Parthian Empire]], succeeded by the [[Sasanian Empire]] in the 2nd century. The Muslim conquest of Persia in the 7th century brought Islamization, and the [[Safavid dynasty]] reunified the country by 1501 and converted it to Shia Islam. After a 1953 coup aided by the US and UK removed an elected prime minister, Iran was ruled as an autocracy under the Shah until the [[Iranian Revolution]] of 1979, which created an Islamic republic. Foreign relations have been shaped by regional conflicts, beginning with the [[Iran–Iraq War]], and by the contentious nuclear program.

Development of the region of [[Mesopotamia]], between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, from prehistory to the present. Sumer, which emerged between 6000 and 5000 BC, is recognized as the world's earliest civilization, with urban development, written language and monumental architecture. The region produced early literature and advances in astronomy and mathematics before the Neo-Babylonian Empire was conquered by [[Cyrus the Great]] in 539 BC. Under the [[Abbasid Caliphate]], Baghdad, founded in 762, became a center of the [[Islamic Golden Age]] until the Mongol invasion of 1258. Ottoman rule lasted until the end of World War I, after which Mandatory Iraq was established under the British. Iraq gained independence in 1932 as a kingdom, which became a republic in 1958. Later challenges included the rule of [[Saddam Hussein]], the US-led [[2003 invasion of Iraq]], sectarian violence and the rise of the [[Islamic State]].

Development of the faith that began with the mission of [[Muhammad]] in [[Mecca]] and [[Medina]] in the early 7th century. After Muhammad's death in 632, the first caliphs unified Arabia and launched conquests that extended Islamic rule from Spain to India by the mid-8th century. The [[Umayyad Caliphate]] ruled from Damascus, and the [[Abbasid Caliphate]] from Baghdad, where the House of Wisdom translated classical learning during the [[Islamic Golden Age]]. A dispute over succession divided Sunnis from Shiites, whose leader Husayn was killed at Karbala in 680. The [[Delhi Sultanate]] conquered northern India in the early 13th century, while Mongol invasions and the [[Black Death]] weakened the traditional centers of the Muslim world. In the early modern period the Ottomans, Timurids, Mughals and Safavids emerged as gunpowder empires. Most of the Muslim world fell under European control in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

Development of the Southern Levant as the land of the Jewish people, from prehistory to the present. Kingdoms of Israel and Judah formed in the Iron Age, and the region was then ruled by [[Assyria]], [[Babylon]], Persia and Greece, followed by the Hasmonean dynasty and the Roman Republic. A Christian majority later emerged under Byzantine rule. After the 7th-century Muslim conquest the region came under caliphates, the [[Crusades]] and Mamluk rule, and four centuries of Ottoman administration. In the 19th century, [[Zionism]] drove increased Jewish immigration. After World War I, Britain administered Palestine under a mandate and committed to a Jewish homeland through the [[Balfour Declaration]]. Tensions led to the 1947 UN Partition Plan and civil war. On May 14, 1948, [[David Ben-Gurion]] proclaimed independence, and the [[1948 Arab–Israeli War]] followed. Peace treaties with Egypt (1979) and Jordan (1994) were signed, and the Oslo I Accord of 1993 established the Palestinian Authority, but the [[Israeli–Palestinian conflict]] remains unresolved.

Development of the Italian peninsula and adjacent islands, from the Paleolithic to the present. The [[Roman Republic]] unified the peninsula before the [[Roman Empire]], established in 27 BC, ruled the Mediterranean for centuries. After the fall of the [[Western Roman Empire]], Italy fragmented into city-states and regional polities, and maritime republics such as [[Venice]] and [[Genoa]] prospered. The [[Renaissance]] spread from these states across Europe. In the 19th century, unification produced a nation-state under the House of Savoy, and the Kingdom of Italy built a colonial empire. Italy was victorious in World War I and acquired Trento and Trieste. The fascist dictatorship of [[Benito Mussolini]] took power in 1922. Italy fought as an Axis power until its surrender and occupation by Nazi Germany, then as a co-belligerent of the Allies. A 1946 referendum abolished the monarchy, and the republic co-founded the European Union and NATO.

Development of the island nation of Japan, from the Paleolithic to the present. The Jōmon period of hunter-gatherers was followed by the Yayoi period, when migrants from the continent introduced iron and agriculture. Between the 4th and 9th centuries, Japan's kingdoms were gradually unified under the emperor. The [[Heian period]] (794–1185) was a golden age of classical culture. The [[Tokugawa shogunate]] ruled the Edo period (1600–1868), cutting off almost all contact with the outside world. The American Perry Expedition of 1853–54 ended that seclusion, and the [[Boshin War]] of 1868 returned power to the emperor. The [[Meiji Restoration]] transformed Japan into a great power. Japan's military dominated politics in the 1920s and 1930s. After the [[Attack on Pearl Harbor]] in 1941, Japan surrendered in 1945 after the [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]]. The 1947 constitution made Japan a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy, and under the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|Liberal Democratic Party]] Japan enjoyed high economic growth after 1955.

Development of the Korean Peninsula and southern Manchuria, from the Lower Paleolithic to the present. According to a mythic account, the Gojoseon kingdom was founded in 2333 BC, and it fell to the Han dynasty of China in the late 2nd century BC. The [[Three Kingdoms of Korea]] of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla controlled the peninsula from 57 BC until Silla unified it in 676. The [[Goryeo]] dynasty unified the peninsula, and Mongol invasions in the 13th century brought it under the [[Mongol Empire]]. In 1392 General Yi Seong-gye founded the [[Joseon]] dynasty, under which King [[Sejong the Great]] personally created [[Hangul]]. Joseon repelled Japanese invasions from 1592 to 1637 with Ming help and the naval fleet of [[Yi Sun-sin]]. Japan annexed Korea in 1910. Division along the 38th parallel after 1945 led to the [[Korean War]] (1950–1953), after which the Republic of Korea industrialized rapidly, while the Democratic People's Republic of Korea became a hereditary dictatorship.
